# Mittavindakajātaka (Ja 369)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mittavindakajātaka* (Ja 369) is a canonical birth story in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon, titled *On Mittavindaka* in English. The narrative framework is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha tells the story regarding an unruly bhikkhu, noting that the fuller background narrative is detailed in the *Mahāmittavinda Jātaka* [Cowell 1897].

In the story, Mittavindaka is cast adrift into the sea as a result of his conduct and visits successive oceanic palaces of crystal, silver, jewels, and gold inhabited by female spirits [JIABS 2013; Cowell 1897]. Driven by insatiable greed and covetousness, he wanders further until he enters the Ussada hell, mistaking it for a wondrous city [Cowell 1897; Winternitz 1933]. There he incurs the punishment of having a razor-sharp wheel (*khuracakka*) revolving upon his head, grinding his skull [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897; Winternitz 1933]. The Bodhisatta, appearing as a visiting deity in the Ussada hell, engages in a verse dialogue with Mittavindaka, declaring that those who abandon celestial joy in pursuit of excessive desire are doomed to become wheel-bearers (*cakkadhārino*) [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. The Buddha concludes by identifying the unruly monk as Mittavindaka and himself as the divine being [Cowell 1897].
